problemText: You are looking at a map and you want to know what the entire map is showing you. Which map part should you read?
choices: the legend, to find out what each symbol represents
the compass rose, to determine which direction is north
the scale bar, to figure out real-world distances between places
the title, to learn the overall subject or location of the map
hints: Think about which part is usually printed near the top of a map.
This part answers the question 'What does this map show?'

problemText: A student is holding a map titled 'Lake District Recreation Map.' On the map, she sees a small blue X symbol that she does not recognize. Where should she look to find out what the blue X stands for on this particular map?
choices: in the legend, where symbols are paired with their meanings for this map
at the compass rose, which shows all four cardinal directions
at the scale bar, which shows how far apart places really are
by remembering what blue X symbols mean on other maps she has seen
hints: Each map creates its own symbols, so you need to check the map in front of you, not a different one.
The part that explains what symbols mean is the one that answers 'What do these symbols mean?'

problemText: On the Mountain Ridge Trail Map, a hiker notices the compass rose shows the arrow labeled N pointing toward the right edge of the page. A shelter symbol sits directly to the left of a water fountain symbol on the page. Based on the compass rose, in which real-world direction is the shelter from the water fountain?
choices: north, because when the compass rose points right, the left side of the page automatically points toward north instead
west, because left on the page means west when that map's compass rose points right for north
south, because the shelter is positioned away from the direction that the compass rose arrow is pointing
east, because the right side of any map page is always considered the east direction in real-world navigation
hints: You must use this map's own compass rose, not what you remember from other maps.
If north points right, then left points in the opposite direction.

problemText: A student wants to plan a camping trip and has two questions: first, 'How far apart are the campsite and the fishing dock on the map?' and second, 'What symbol does the map use to mark a ranger station?' The student starts to answer both questions by reading the scale bar. Explain why reading only the scale bar will answer one question but not the other. Which question is which?
choices: The scale bar answers the ranger station question because the names of all symbols are listed along the edges of the scale bar on most maps.
The scale bar answers both questions equally well because it contains all the information needed to interpret everything shown on any map.
The scale bar answers the distance question, but you need to read the legend to find out what symbol marks a ranger station, because the legend is what explains what symbols mean.
The scale bar answers only the ranger station question because the bar marks themselves are designed to show what each symbol represents on the map.
hints: Remember: each map part answers its own specific question, not all questions.
The scale bar shows distances, and the legend shows what symbols mean—these are two different jobs.

problemText: On the Willow Creek Park Map, a hiker reads the compass rose and sees that north points toward the bottom of the page. Later, the hiker notices two locations on the map: a picnic table directly above a parking lot on the page itself. The hiker concludes: 'The parking lot must be north of the picnic table.' Is this conclusion correct? Explain by referring to the compass rose and what it means.
choices: Yes, the conclusion is correct because things directly above other things on a map are always north.
Yes, the conclusion is correct because the title tells you that Willow Creek Park is in the north.
No, the conclusion is wrong because the compass rose on this map shows that down on the page is north, so directly above on the page means south, not north.
No, the conclusion is wrong because the scale bar does not confirm the direction.
hints: The compass rose tells you what direction each part of the page points to for this particular map.
If the compass rose shows north pointing down, then 'above on the page' points toward the top, which is the opposite of north.

problemText: A student is reading two different maps: Map A shows 'Pine Valley State Park' with a scale bar marked 0 to 5 miles, and Map B shows 'Oak Ridge County' with a scale bar marked 0 to 50 miles. The student measures a straight-line distance of 2 inches on both maps and uses each map's scale bar to find the real-world distance. Will the student find that 2 inches stands for the same real-world distance on both maps? Use the information from the lesson to explain your reasoning.
choices: No, because each map has its own scale bar, and the marks on one map's scale bar do not mean the same thing as the marks on another map's scale bar. A 2-inch line on a map showing 50 miles per bar segment stands for a much larger real-world distance than a 2-inch line on a map showing 5 miles per bar segment.
Yes, because inches are always the same measurement, so 2 inches will always stand for the same real-world distance no matter which map you measure on.
No, because the titles of the maps are different, which means they were created by different mapmakers and therefore use different measurement systems.
Yes, because the scale bar is a standard tool that all mapmakers use in exactly the same way, so the relationship between page length and real-world distance stays constant across all maps.
hints: Remember: each map picks its own scale bar marks, just like each map picks its own symbols for the legend.
The scale bar connects a length on the page to a real-world distance, and those marks are different from map to map.

problemText: A mapmaker is building a map whose legend shows different colors for each country and a star symbol marking the capital city of each country. What is the main job of this map?
choices: To show human-made boundaries such as country borders and the names and locations of capital cities
To show how high or low the land sits in different parts of each country using elevation colors and contour lines
To show how one piece of information, such as rainfall or population density, changes across the countries using shading patterns
To show rivers, lakes, and mountain peaks without any human-made borders or political boundaries marked
hints: Look at what the legend lists: country colors and capital-city symbols.
Ask yourself: does this legend tell you about the shape of the land, or about human-made places and borders?

problemText: A geography student needs to find out which parts of a region receive the most rainfall and which parts receive the least. The student's legend shows light green for areas getting under 15 inches of rain per year, medium blue for 15 to 40 inches, and dark blue for more than 40 inches. Why is this map the right choice for the student's question?
choices: Because it shows country borders so the student can see which countries are in the region
Because it uses one chosen kind of information—rainfall amounts—spread across different areas to answer the question
Because it shows elevation colors that tell the student how mountainous each area is
Because it marks capital cities with special symbols so the student can locate the biggest population centers
hints: The student's question is about one specific topic: how much rain falls in different places.
Which map type is built to show one chosen kind of data spread across an area?

problemText: A teacher shows two students different maps of the same country. One map's legend lists green for low elevation and brown for high elevation, with symbols for mountain peaks and rivers. The other map's legend lists a different flat color for each province and black lines showing where province borders are drawn. Which map should a student use to find out where the mountains and valleys are located in that country?
choices: The map with the province colors and black border lines, because borders always mark where the land changes
The map with elevation colors and mountain symbols, because it shows the natural shape of the land
Either map would work equally well, because they both show the country
The map with the province colors, because flat colors are always used to show natural features
hints: Think about what each legend is built to show: one shows human-made boundaries, the other shows how high the land sits.
Which map type uses color to stand for elevation and includes symbols for natural features like mountains and rivers?

problemText: A mapmaker creates three different maps of the same desert region. Map 1's legend shows country borders and capital cities. Map 2's legend shows colors for elevation and symbols for oases and salt flats. Map 3's legend shows different colors representing the percentage of people who speak Arabic as their main language in each area. A visitor to this region wants to understand both the natural landscape and the human geography. Why would the visitor need to look at more than one of these maps to get a complete picture?
choices: Because Map 1 shows all the natural features, so the other maps are unnecessary additions
Because each map shows a different main job, and no single map is built to show both natural landscape and human data at the same time
Because maps with borders are always more accurate than maps with colors for elevation
Because physical maps and thematic maps always show the same information in different colors
hints: Recall the lesson idea: every map is built around one main job, and a map cannot show everything without becoming confusing.
Map 1 is political, Map 2 is physical, and Map 3 is thematic. What does each one show, and what does each one leave out?

problemText: A student is looking at a map and says: "This map has different colors spread all over it, so it must be a physical map showing elevation." But the legend actually lists light brown for areas where cattle are raised, tan for areas where sheep are raised, and cream for areas where goats are raised. What is wrong with the student's reasoning, and what kind of map is this actually?
choices: This is actually a thematic map, because the colors represent one chosen topic—the type of livestock raised—spread across the area, not elevation
This is actually a political map, because livestock colors are used instead of country borders to show human activities
The student's reasoning is correct; this is a physical map with elevation, just using unusual colors instead of the typical green and brown
The student made no mistake; any map with multiple colors must be a physical map
hints: The key question is not 'does the map use color?' but 'what does that color represent in the legend?'
Physical-map colors stand for elevation. What do these colors actually stand for?

problemText: A geographer has three maps of West Africa side by side. Map X shows country borders with each country in a different flat color and capital cities marked with a star. Map Y shows green and yellow colors representing low elevation, tan for medium elevation, and dark red for high elevation, plus blue symbols for rivers. Map Z shows only two colors: light orange for areas where fewer than 500,000 people live, and dark orange for areas where 500,000 or more people live. A student needs to complete three different tasks: (1) find the location of major mountain ranges, (2) find which country contains a capital city, and (3) find which areas are most densely populated. Which map should the student use for each task, and why would using the wrong map for any task make the answer unclear or impossible to find?
choices: For all three tasks, use Map X, because it shows the complete picture of the region in a single map with all information available

Use Map Y for task 1 because its legend lists elevation; use Map X for task 2 because its legend marks capital cities with symbols; use Map Z for task 3 because its colors show where the most people live in each area
Use Map Y for all tasks, because physical maps show every kind of information geographers need to know
Use Map X for tasks 1 and 2, and Map Z for task 3, because political maps include some natural features along with human features
hints: Remember that each map type shows one main job in its legend. Match each task to the map whose legend includes that information.
Map X is political (borders and capitals), Map Y is physical (elevation and rivers), and Map Z is thematic (population). Which legend contains the data each task requires?

problemText: According to the lesson, what is a continent? Which of the following correctly defines the term as it is used in this course?
choices: A body of salt water that covers most of Earth's surface.
One of Earth's largest continuous areas of land.
A narrow strip of land that connects two larger landmasses.
Any area of land that is surrounded by ocean on all sides.
hints: The lesson defines both continents and oceans separately, using the word 'largest' and 'continuous' for both.
Think about whether the definition should describe land or water.

problemText: You are describing the location of Africa to a friend who cannot see a map. Using the two-question routine from the lesson, you first ask what touches Africa along its edges. Which of the following correctly identifies Africa's neighbors?
choices: The Atlantic Ocean to the west, the Indian Ocean to the east, and Europe to the north, with no land connection to Asia.
The Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, and the Pacific Ocean to the south.
The Atlantic Ocean to the west, the Indian Ocean to the east, the Mediterranean Sea to the north, and Asia joined by a narrow strip of land.
The Pacific Ocean to the east, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, and South America connected by land to the south.
hints: Africa touches two oceans on its sides and has a specific land neighbor to its east; the lesson states this connection explicitly.
Remember that three continents sit on one continuous landmass even though they are counted separately.

problemText: A student claims that Australia is joined to Asia by a narrow strip of land, the same way North America and South America are connected. Is this claim correct, and why or why not?
choices: Yes, it is correct; the lesson lists Australia as one of the seven continents, so it must be connected to another continent like all the others.
No, it is not correct; Australia stands alone as an island continent surrounded entirely by ocean, with the Indian Ocean to its west and the Pacific Ocean to its east.
Yes, it is correct; both Australia and North America are large continents, so they must both have land connections to their neighbors.
No, it is not correct; Australia is actually separated from Asia by the Atlantic Ocean, not connected by land.
hints: The lesson specifically states which continents have land connections and which ones stand alone surrounded by ocean.
Think about what the lesson says is between Australia and other continents — water, land, or neither.

problemText: Using the two-question routine to describe the Pacific Ocean's location: the Pacific touches the Americas on one side and Asia and Australia on the other. If the Pacific Ocean lies west of Asia, then what direction must Asia lie relative to the Pacific Ocean, and why does checking this direction matter?
choices: Asia must lie east of the Pacific Ocean; flipping the relationship like this catches if a direction was written backward.
Asia must lie south of the Pacific Ocean; this confirms the ocean separates two continents completely.
Asia must lie north of the Pacific Ocean; this proves the lesson's description is the only true way to divide the world.
Asia must lie west of the Pacific Ocean; flipping it shows the two regions are actually on the same landmass.
hints: The lesson teaches that flipping a position statement is a way to check that directions are not backward — think about what 'west of' becomes when you flip it.
When you reverse a direction relationship, the directions swap but the fact that they touch remains true.

problemText: The lesson states that Europe and Asia sit on one continuous landmass with no ocean between them, yet geographers still count them as two separate continents. Which of the following best explains why a continent can be defined as a separate entity even when it is joined by land to another continent?
choices: The lesson defines continents solely by size, so any landmass larger than a certain threshold must be counted as its own continent.
A convention is an agreed-upon way of dividing something; continents are divided by convention rather than by natural boundaries like water.
Continents are always separated from one another by either an ocean or a sea, except in the special case of Europe and Asia.
The two-question routine requires that every continent be surrounded by at least one ocean, so Europe and Asia are only counted as separate because each borders its own body of water.
hints: The lesson introduces the word 'convention' and explains that it means a group has agreed on a way to divide something that could have been done differently.
Notice that the lesson says some geographers combine Europe and Asia into one continent — this shows the division is a choice, not a fact of nature.

problemText: A student states: 'The four oceans are separate bodies of water divided by walls, just like the seven continents are separate because water or land separates them.' Identify what is wrong with this claim, explain what is actually true about the oceans according to the lesson, and describe how the two-question routine for oceans differs from its use for continents because of this fact.
choices: The claim is wrong because oceans have no walls; they are one connected body of water divided by name rather than by barriers, so the two-question routine asks what continents touch an ocean's edges, not what walls surround it.
The claim is wrong because there are actually five oceans, not four, and the Southern Ocean is the largest; the two-question routine treats oceans as separate in all other respects.
The claim is wrong because oceans do have walls made of continents; the two-question routine asks which oceans touch a continent's edges, not which continents touch an ocean's edges.
The claim is wrong because most continents are not separated by water; the two-question routine works differently for oceans because they are named by geographers rather than occurring naturally.
hints: The lesson explicitly states that the four oceans are one connected body of water divided by name, not divided by physical barriers or walls.
When applying the two-question routine, think about what the routine actually asks: what does a feature touch along its edges, and in which direction?

problemText: The word hemisphere comes from two parts: 'hemi' and 'sphere.' What does the word hemisphere mean?
choices: A line that runs around the middle of Earth
An imaginary circle that divides Earth into east and west
Half of Earth
The area between the North Pole and the South Pole
hints: Think about what 'hemi' means and what 'sphere' means.
The lesson breaks apart the word into its two pieces.

problemText: A pilot flying over the Atlantic Ocean crosses a line running east to west that divides the Northern Hemisphere from the Southern Hemisphere. Which line has the pilot just crossed?
choices: The Prime Meridian
A line invented by pilots for navigation
The boundary between Europe and Africa
The Equator
hints: Recall which line decides whether a place is north or south of something.
This line runs east to west all the way around Earth at its widest part.

problemText: A whale in the ocean is swimming west and crosses an imaginary line running from the North Pole to the South Pole. This line passes through Greenwich, England. After crossing, the whale is now west of this line. Which hemisphere has the whale entered?
choices: The Western Hemisphere
The Southern Hemisphere
The Northern Hemisphere
The Eastern Hemisphere
hints: The line that runs from pole to pole through Greenwich is the Prime Meridian.
Crossing west of this line puts you on the west side of it.

problemText: A research team collects samples at a location. They record that the location is south of the Equator and east of the Prime Meridian. Using the two-question method taught in class, which pair of hemispheres describes this location?
choices: The Northern Hemisphere and the Eastern Hemisphere
The Southern Hemisphere and the Eastern Hemisphere
The Southern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere
The Northern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere
hints: Always ask question 1 first: is it north or south of the Equator?
Then ask question 2: is it east or west of the Prime Meridian?

problemText: Two students are debating where South America is located. Student A says, 'South America must be in the Southern Hemisphere only, because it is called South America.' Student B says, 'South America is in two hemispheres, one from each pair.' Which student is correct, and why?
choices: Student A is correct; the name tells you which hemisphere it is in.
Student B is correct; a place sits in two hemispheres, one from the north-south pair and one from the east-west pair.
Both are partially correct; South America is in multiple hemispheres depending on which part you measure.
Neither is correct; hemispheres are only for oceans, not continents.
hints: Remember that every place on Earth (except points exactly on a line) sits in two hemispheres.
You must run both questions—the north-south question and the east-west question—on every place.

problemText: A geography class studies four continents: North America lies entirely north of the Equator and entirely west of the Prime Meridian. South America has land both north and south of the Equator, but all of it is west of the Prime Meridian. Asia has land both north and south of the Equator and land both east and west of the Prime Meridian. Antarctica lies entirely south of the Equator and entirely east of the Prime Meridian. Which continent has land in all four hemispheres?
choices: North America, because it is the largest
South America, because it has two different latitudes
Antarctica, because it is farthest south
Asia, because both lines cross through it
hints: For a place to be in all four hemispheres, both the Equator and the Prime Meridian must cross through it.
Check each continent: does the Equator run across it, and does the Prime Meridian run across it?
